amendments.rule: In a construct chain, the English relational expression belongs to the nomen rectum, headed on that noun. This is normally *of*, handled exactly as a Greek genitive `of + noun`, but where the ASV recasts the construct relation with *from*, *for*, *in*, *to*, *over*, or another preposition, that expression belongs there too. The construct state of the first noun is what signals the relation, but the first noun's unit takes only its own English word. **The rectum may be a pronominal suffix rather than a noun, and nothing changes.** Where the ASV renders such a suffix not with a possessive but with *of* and a pronoun — `כֻּלָּם` → *all of them*, `מַרְבִּיתָם` → *the greatest part of them* — the whole *of + pronoun* is the suffix's one unit, headed on the pronoun under rule 24, and the construct noun keeps only its own word: `כֹּל` takes *all*, never *all of*. Do not read that *of* as part of an English quantifier or as licensed by the construct noun's own state, for the reason this rule's third sentence gives. The corpus aligns a suffix to *of them* headed on *them* in 116 units and records no `כֹּל` → *all of* treatment, and where the construct noun's own English is something else the division shows in a single unit: `כֻּלָּם` → *five of them in all* gives *in all* to `כֹּל` and *of them* to the suffix. Where the ASV writes a possessive or a bare pronoun instead, rule 18 governs as before and there is no *of* to place. **But a preposition that renders the construct noun's own lexeme is that noun's rendering and not the relation's.** Where the first noun is itself a directional or relational word and the ASV spends its one English word on that lexeme instead of writing a noun for it — `דֶּרֶךְ הַצָּפוֹן` → *toward the north*, `דֶּרֶךְ הַקָּדִים` → *toward the east* — the preposition belongs to the construct noun and heads its unit, while the rectum takes only its own word and the rectum's article takes the written *the* under rule 29. Decide it by the subtraction test rules 16, 31 and 43 use: drop the English preposition and ask whether the construct noun has lost its whole rendering or only the relation between the two nouns has gone. Where the construct noun would be left with nothing at all, the word is its own and this rule's first sentence does not reach it; where the construct noun keeps an English word of its own — `דֶּרֶךְ אַמָּה אֶחָת` → *a way of one cubit* — the first sentence stands and the *of* goes to the rectum. Do not mark such a construct `unrepresented` in order to give its preposition to the rectum: that leaves a lexical noun holding a plain English rendering unaligned, against rule 2. The corpus renders a construct `דֶּרֶךְ` by *toward*, *is toward* or *was toward* in eighteen units, always headed on the preposition, and records no unit where the rectum of such a phrase holds the preposition while the construct goes unrepresented. Two riders. Where a Hebrew preposition stands before such a construct noun and the ASV writes a single English word for the pair, rule 30 fuses them instead, as `לִפְנֵי` → *before*; and where the phrase is the predicate of a verbless clause the construction-supplied copula joins the construct noun's unit under rule 20, as `דֶּרֶךְ הַצָּפוֹן` → *were toward the north*. **And a second `דֶּרֶךְ` standing in the same phrase is not a repetition the ASV renders once.** `הַדֶּרֶךְ דֶּרֶךְ הַצָּפוֹן` → *the way toward the north* gives *the way* to the absolute, with its article taking the *the*, and *toward* to the construct, and rule 22 reaches neither, because each has an English word of its own.
amendments.why: Rule 19's second sentence, read alone, sends any preposition that recasts a construct relation to the rectum, and it misled this chapter at EZK.42.1: the accepted alignment marked the construct דֶּרֶךְ `unrepresented` and gave *toward* to הַצָּפוֹן on that authority, which the verse pass had to correct. The corpus contradicts that reading — a construct דֶּרֶךְ is aligned to *toward* in 13 units, *is toward* in 4 (EZK.40.20, 40.22) and *was toward* in 1 (EZK.40.44), always headed on the preposition, and the single unrepresented דֶּרֶךְ in the corpus (PSA.107.17) is one where מִן took *because of* and no rectum holds a preposition. The added clause is a qualification of the rule that was wrong, not a cross-reference, so it replaces rule 19's text whole; the subtraction test keeps the original sentence governing every chain where the construct noun keeps an English word of its own, as `דֶּרֶךְ אַמָּה אֶחָת` → *a way of one cubit* does in EZK.42.4. The last clause is added because rule 22 is the other rule a later pass reaches for when two דֶּרֶךְ tokens stand together, and EZK.42.1 shows that it does not apply when the ASV writes an English word for each.

conventions: A doubled סָבִיב סָבִיב that the ASV renders once by the compound adverb *round about* takes both English words on the first occurrence, and the second occurrence is `unrepresented` under rule 22. So EZK.42.15 and EZK.42.20, which agree. Rule 22 says which occurrence is the rendered one only for a counted noun distributed across a numeral, so it does not settle this; the compound adverb is one rendering of one adverb and is not divided across the two tokens, which is the competing reading each unit's note names.

In a verbless clause opening with a locative prepositional phrase, read whether the clause predicates a location of a definite subject or asserts existence, and place the construction-supplied copula accordingly. EZK.42.9, whose subject הַמֵּבִיא is articular and for which the ASV writes a bare *was*, is a locative predication, so the copula joins the fronted preposition under rule 49. EZK.42.10, whose subject לְשָׁכוֹת is anarthrous and for which the ASV writes the presentative *there were*, is existential, so the whole frame joins the nominal anchor under rule 20. Rule 20 allows the frame on either a nominal anchor or a prepositional predicate and gives no test for choosing, so this is the chapter's; EZK.40.44 (`לִשְׁכוֹת` → *were chambers* after a fronted מִחוּצָה phrase) reads an indefinite subject the same way.

Where coordinated comparanda each carry their own מִן and the ASV writes the comparison once — מֵהַתַּחְתֹּנוֹת וּמֵהַתִּיכֹנוֹת → *more than from the lower and the middlemost* — the מִן standing on the phrase the English *more than* or *from* introduces takes that English and the later one is `unrepresented` under rule 22, exactly as rule 47 reads which word a single written *the* stands before. So EZK.42.5 (three מִן, two renderings) and EZK.42.6 (three מִן, two renderings). This is what the two BSB מֵ disagreements are; BSB attaches each preposition to its own phrase by documented convention, and neither is an error.

report: Read all 37 candidate lemma groups plus the full verse dump end to end. Every multi-treatment bucket is accounted for by what the ASV writes, or by a morpheme present in one context and absent in the other. No cross-verse split found; patches is empty.

דֶּרֶךְ is the chapter's governing decision and it holds across every verse that has one: the construct דֶּרֶךְ before a direction noun takes the ASV's *toward* itself (with the construction-supplied copula where it is the predicate, 42.11/.12/.15), the absolute or adverbial דֶּרֶךְ takes *way* (42.1, 42.4, 42.11, 42.12, 42.15), the rectum takes only the direction word and its article takes the written *the*. 42.1 writes both tokens and gives each its own English, which is why rule 22 reaches neither.

The four מָדַד verses are not a split. 42.18 writes אֵת on the measured object, so the marker takes the *on* by which the English verb reaches it (rule 16); 42.16 and 42.17 write a bare object with no marker and no preposition, so the *on* joins the verb (rule 44). Rule 44's own limit names this distinction, and both verses' notes flag it.

The candidate table is blind to `added` units, so I checked the five by hand: 42.6 *the uppermost*, 42.11 italic *the way of*, 42.12 appositional *even*, 42.13 and 42.19 connective *and*. Each is a supplied English word with no morpheme standing in its clause, and nowhere else in the chapter is such a word folded into a neighbouring unit — so the table's blind spot is hiding nothing here.

42.9 and 42.10 both open a verbless clause with a locative prepositional phrase and place the copula differently. The difference is licensed and I did not patch it: 42.9 has an articular subject (הַמֵּבִיא) and a bare *was*, a locative predication whose copula goes to the fronted preposition under rule 49; 42.10 has an anarthrous subject and the presentative *there were*, an existential whose frame goes to the nominal anchor under rule 20. Rule 20 explicitly permits either and supplies no test, so the test is recorded as a convention.

BSB: none of the 18 disagreements is a genuine error. The 12 Td are the documented article convention (rule 47 agreement articles, and rule 29's demonstrative phrase in 42.9); the two מֵ are coordinated comparatives the ASV renders once (rule 22); the 42.14 suffix is resumed by the explicit *the priests*; the 42.15 waw is an apodosis waw with no connective written; the two סָבִיב are the second of a doubled adverb. No accepted edge was changed.

One promotion, returned as an amendment to rule 19 rather than a new rule: rule 19's second sentence sends a preposition that recasts a construct relation to the rectum, and in this chapter it did mislead — 42.1's accepted alignment marked the construct דֶּרֶךְ unrepresented and gave *toward* to הַצָּפוֹן before the verse pass corrected it. The corpus renders a construct דֶּרֶךְ by *toward*, *is toward* or *was toward* in eighteen units, always headed on the preposition, and records no unit reading it the other way.
